strengths: Clean architectural idea: augmenting every transformer layer with a dedicated, bounded external memory track (mem2tok/tok2mem cross-attention plus an LRU-based replace/blend update) that is simple to implement and interpret.

Provides a theoretical analysis (exponential forgetting, half-life, boundedness) that gives some formal grounding to the design choices of the LRU update rule, unlike most memory-augmented RL papers that are purely empirical.

Broad empirical coverage across three qualitatively different testbeds (synthetic T-Maze, 48 POPGym tasks, MIKASA-Robo visual manipulation), with a reasonably diverse baseline set (DT, RATE, DMamba, BC, CQL, DP).

Strong extrapolation results on T-Maze (100% success up to 1M-step corridors from L=10, S=3 training) and a fairly thorough ablation study isolating memory size, blending factor, initialization, and segment configuration.

Reports efficiency numbers (parameter count, inference latency) showing the memory mechanism adds little overhead versus DT/RATE, and includes a sanity check on CartPole-v1 confirming memory does not hurt fully observable performance.
weaknesses: Inconsistent reporting of POPGym results: the abstract/main text claims ELMUR is best on '24 of 48' tasks ('more than half'), while the actual Table 4 caption states results on 21 tasks with ELMUR best on only 12 — these numbers should match and the discrepancy undermines confidence in the reported headline claim.

The T-Maze task requires retaining only a single binary cue, so the '100,000x' and 'one million steps' claims, while striking, may be an artifact of the task's minimal information content (LRU memory with enough capacity trivially solves single-bit recall); it is unclear this generalizes to tasks requiring richer, evolving memory content.

The ablation shows that removing the MoE-FFN and replacing it with a plain MLP-FFN preserves accuracy exactly (1.00 vs 1.00) while improving efficiency, which undercuts the motivation for including DeepSeek-MoE in the main architecture and suggests the design choice is not well justified by the evidence presented.

Memory capacity M must be matched to the (often unknown a priori) number of segments N required to solve a task, as shown starkly in the ablations (Figure 6c-d); this is a practical limitation for real-world deployment where horizon length is not known in advance, and the paper does not propose or test any adaptive/growing memory scheme.

Many individual results have large variance/overlapping error bars relative to baselines (e.g., TakeItBack RATE 0.42±0.24 vs ELMUR 0.78±0.03; several POPGym tasks where RATE or BC-LSTM outperform ELMUR), and only 3–4 seeds per condition are used, limiting statistical confidence in the 'consistent' superiority claims.

MIKASA-Robo evaluation is limited to only 4 tasks from one benchmark family, and absolute success rates remain fairly low (0.19–0.89), so the 'nearly doubles baseline performance' claim, while numerically true in places, describes modest absolute capability on manipulation under visual partial observability.

The relative bias mechanism clamps offsets to a fixed maximum distance Dmax, which is in tension with the paper's headline claims of unbounded/arbitrary-horizon generalization — the practical bounds and behavior beyond Dmax are not clearly discussed.

Baseline sets are inconsistent across benchmarks (e.g., RMT and TrXL appear only in the T-Maze figure but not in the POPGym/MIKASA-Robo tables), making cross-benchmark comparisons of relative strength harder to interpret.

No real-robot or online-RL evaluation is provided (acknowledged as a limitation), and the offline imitation-learning setup with expert-generated datasets may not fully capture challenges of noisier, more realistic data regimes.

strengths: The core architectural idea—giving every transformer layer its own persistent, bounded external memory with dedicated read (mem2tok) and write (tok2mem) cross-attention paths plus an LRU-based replace/blend update—is a clean and interpretable mechanism for extending effective context without quadratic cost.
The paper provides a simple theoretical analysis (exponential forgetting, half-life, boundedness) that gives some formal grounding for the memory dynamics, even if the proofs are elementary.
Evaluation spans three qualitatively different benchmark families (synthetic T-Maze, 48 POPGym tasks, visual MIKASA-Robo manipulation), which is a reasonably broad testbed for partial observability.

The T-Maze extrapolation experiment (train at short horizons, evaluate at up to 1M steps) is a striking demonstration of the segment-recurrent memory mechanism generalizing far beyond training length.
Reasonable ablation sweep over memory size, blending factor, initialization scale, and segmentation that clarifies failure modes when memory capacity is insufficient.
weaknesses: The headline POPGym claim ('outperforms baselines on more than half the tasks', 'top score on 24 of 48') is not strongly supported by the paper's own Table 4/2: ELMUR's aggregate return (10.41) is only marginally better than the much simpler RATE baseline (9.54), and on many individual tasks (e.g., BattleshipEasy, MineSweeperEasy/Medium/Hard, ConcentrationEasy, PositionOnlyPendulum*, CountRecallEasy) ELMUR is tied with or actually worse than RATE or BC-LSTM. This undercuts the central robustness claim and suggests the architectural additions bring limited net benefit on this benchmark.

All methods, including ELMUR, remain far below the PPO-GRU expert on most POPGym puzzle tasks (e.g., sum of returns 10.41 vs expert 16.51), meaning the 'robust memory under partial observability' claim is only weakly demonstrated in absolute terms, despite relative improvements over weak baselines.

The baseline set is dated and somewhat weak for a 2025 memory/long-horizon paper: comparisons are limited to DT, RATE, DMamba, BC, CQL, and Diffusion Policy. Several directly relevant and more recent memory-augmented architectures discussed extensively in the related work (Titans, AMAGO-2, Re:Frame, Memorizing/Compressive/Block-Recurrent Transformers, RMT-style approaches shown only in the T-Maze figure) are not compared on POPGym or MIKASA-Robo, making it hard to judge whether ELMUR's gains are due to the specific LRU/dual-track design or simply more parameters/compute.

The T-Maze and generalization experiments use very small, almost toy configurations (context length 10, memory size as low as 2 slots per the hyperparameter table), and the task itself is a single binary-choice recall problem; a 100% success rate across all lengths for ELMUR (while other baselines degrade) is a strong claim but the benchmark may be too simple/saturated to meaningfully validate real long-horizon credit assignment, especially given no analysis of when/why ELMUR might fail.

The MoE-FFN component, motivated at length in Section 3 as a design choice (contrasted against standard DT MLP FFNs), is shown in the ablation (Table 3) to be unnecessary — replacing MoE with a plain MLP preserves accuracy while improving efficiency — indicating this part of the architecture is not actually a meaningful contribution and is somewhat over-sold in the method description.

Architecturally, ELMUR is a fairly incremental combination of well-established ideas: segment-level recurrence (Transformer-XL/RMT), explicit external memory with read/write attention (Memory Networks/NTM/DNC/Memformer), relative positional bias (Transformer-XL), and LRU-style cache replacement — the novelty lies mainly in combining these per-layer rather than at the sequence level, which is a modest conceptual step.

MIKASA-Robo evaluation is limited to only 4 tasks from one suite, and absolute success rates for the harder tasks (RememberColor5/9) remain low (0.19–0.23), so 'nearly doubles baseline performance' is from a very low absolute base and does not demonstrate practical competence on the underlying manipulation problem.

Statistical reporting is based on only 3 (or 4) seeds with fairly high variance in several cells (e.g., RATE on TakeItBack: 0.42±0.24), raising concerns about the robustness of some comparative claims, particularly where margins between methods are small.

No real-robot or even higher-fidelity simulation validation is provided; the entire evaluation is offline imitation learning from scripted/PPO-expert data in simplified simulators, which limits the demonstrated significance for 'real-world robotic agents' as claimed in the abstract/introduction.

strengths: The architecture (ELMUR) is clearly motivated and well described, with a principled design combining per-layer external memory, bidirectional cross-attention (mem2tok/tok2mem), relative temporal bias, and LRU-based update/rewrite for bounded capacity.

Solid theoretical grounding: formal propositions on exponential forgetting (with half-life derivation) and memory boundedness under convex updates, which connect cleanly to the LRU mechanism and are proven rigorously in the appendix.

Broad empirical evaluation across three distinct regimes (synthetic T-Maze, 48-task POPGym suite, and visual sparse-reward MIKASA-Robo manipulation), testing both retention and generalization across sequence lengths.

Striking results on T-Maze: 100% success up to corridor lengths of 1,000,000 steps with a context window of only 10 and perfect generalization across train/test length combinations (Figure 4), demonstrating the memory mechanism truly extends beyond the attention window.

Reasonable efficiency profile: ELMUR runs faster per step than RATE and DT despite comparable or larger parameter counts, attributed to bounded memory size and MoE FFNs rather than full sequence-length dependent attention cost.
Useful ablation study isolating the roles of memory capacity (M), blending factor (λ), initialization, relative bias, LRU, and shared vs. per-layer memory, which supports the design choices made.
Good coverage of related work situating the contribution against memory-augmented transformers, state-space models, and VLA/manipulation literature.
weaknesses: There is an unresolved inconsistency between the claimed POPGym coverage: abstract/intro state ELMUR 'obtains the top score on 24 of 48 POPGym tasks' and RQ4 references 'Table 4' for 'full results', yet Table 4 and its caption explicitly cover only 21 tasks (claiming best on 12 of 21), leaving the source of the '24 of 48' claim unverifiable from the presented tables, which undermines confidence in the headline comparative claim.

Baseline sets are inconsistent across experiments: T-Maze (Figure 3) includes RMT, TrXL, and DMamba, but the POPGym leaderboard (Tables 2 and 4) and MIKASA-Robo table (Table 1) drop DMamba, RMT, and TrXL entirely without explanation, making it hard to assess whether ELMUR's advantage holds against the strongest alternatives in each domain.

On POPGym's puzzle subset, ELMUR's absolute aggregated score (1.2) remains far below the PPO-GRU expert's puzzle performance, and many individual puzzle tasks (e.g., Autoencode*, Battleship*, Concentration*, MineSweeper*) show ELMUR scoring far below the expert, suggesting the gains over baselines are partly driven by weak baselines rather than genuinely strong absolute puzzle-solving memory capability.

No real-robot or non-simulated validation, and no online RL comparisons, which limits claims about real-world applicability of the proposed memory mechanism in robotics despite framing the paper strongly around robotic manipulation.

The headline '100,000x longer than attention window' claim is demonstrated on a T-Maze task where only a single early cue needs to be retained verbatim, which is a relatively low-complexity memory requirement (one bit of information); it is unclear how this striking extrapolation number generalizes to tasks requiring richer, evolving memory content, as reflected by the much smaller and more mixed gains on POPGym puzzles and MIKASA-Robo RememberColor5/9.

Statistical rigor is uneven: POPGym aggregate tables (Table 2) report point estimates without uncertainty, and some per-task standard errors in Table 4 are overlapping between ELMUR and baselines (e.g., HigherLower*, VelocityOnlyCartpole*), making several 'wins' only marginal or within noise.

The ablation study (RQ5) is conducted on a single task (RememberColor3-v0), limiting the generality of conclusions about component contributions (e.g., LRU vs. relative bias importance) across the broader benchmark suite.

MoE-FFN is introduced as a core architectural choice but the ablation (MoE→MLP) shows no accuracy difference while claiming efficiency gains, raising the question of whether MoE provides any real benefit for the model scales studied, beyond added complexity.

strengths: Proposes a well-motivated architecture (ELMUR) that equips every transformer layer with its own external memory track, bidirectional mem2tok/tok2mem cross-attention, and a principled LRU-based update rule (replacement + convex blending), addressing a clear gap in long-horizon partially observable decision making.

Provides rigorous theoretical analysis (Propositions 1 and 2) with full proofs establishing exponential forgetting rates, half-life bounds, and boundedness of memory embeddings under the convex update rule, connecting theory to the empirically observed retention horizons.

Extremely broad empirical evaluation spanning synthetic T-Maze (up to 1M-step corridors, 100,000x context extension), 48 POPGym tasks, 32 MIKASA-Robo visual manipulation tasks, D4RL MuJoCo MDPs, and ViZDoom-Two-Colors 3D navigation, with strong and consistent baselines (DT, RATE, DMamba, CQL, DP, BC).

Very thorough ablation and interpretability studies in the appendix (memory probing with linear classifiers, PCA analysis, cross-attention visualization, memory update pattern heatmaps) that provide compelling mechanistic evidence that the model performs genuine, causally relevant long-term storage rather than merely benefiting from added parameters.

Reasonable efficiency profile relative to baselines (comparable parameter count, faster per-step latency than RATE/DT) despite the added memory machinery, and inclusion of an MoE-vs-MLP ablation showing efficiency gains without accuracy loss.
Reproducibility statement, detailed hyperparameter tables, and stated code/data availability support replication.
weaknesses: Reported POPGym results are internally inconsistent: the main text/abstract claims a top score on '24 of 48' (also stated as 'more than half') tasks, while the caption of the detailed results table (Table 5) states ELMUR is best on '12' of '21 partially observable tasks,' and the aggregate score table differs slightly (9.5/10.4 vs 9.54/10.41) — this discrepancy undermines confidence in the reported comparative statistics.

On MIKASA-Robo, a large fraction of tasks (BunchOfColors, SeqOfColors, ChainOfColors — 9 of 32 tasks) show 0.00 success for every method including ELMUR, meaning the headline '21 of 23 tasks' and '~70% aggregate improvement' claims are computed only over a subset of tasks where any method succeeds at all, which could overstate the practical significance of the gains and obscures that a third of the tasks remain entirely unsolved by all approaches.

On POPGym reactive/control tasks, ELMUR's advantage over DT/RATE/BC-LSTM is marginal (9.2 vs 9.1–9.3), and it is not uniformly the best method across categories, suggesting the gains are concentrated in memory-intensive puzzle tasks rather than a universal improvement.

The dramatic '100,000x' extrapolation claim is derived from a specific favorable configuration (L=10, S=3) on a synthetic, low-dimensional T-Maze task; the practical relevance of such extreme extrapolation to realistic robotic settings with rich, noisy, high-dimensional observations is not established, and no similarly extreme long-horizon stress test is performed on MIKASA-Robo or real-world-like data.

The architecture adds non-trivial complexity (per-layer memory tracks, dual cross-attention blocks, LRU bookkeeping with anchors, MoE FFNs, relative-bias tables) relative to simpler baselines like RATE or DT, and while latency is reported as comparable, a more complete compute/memory-footprint comparison (e.g., training time, FLOPs, wall-clock scaling with M and number of layers) is not provided.

No real-robot or truly high-fidelity long-horizon manipulation benchmark is used (acknowledged as a limitation), and comparisons to more recent, directly competing memory-augmented VLA/manipulation methods discussed in related work (e.g., MemoryVLA, SAM2Act+) are only qualitative, not empirical, leaving open how ELMUR compares to the most relevant contemporary memory-augmented manipulation baselines.

The ablation study's reported 'Score' metric (Table 3) is not clearly defined (e.g., which exact metric, over how many seeds, and whether it matches the success-rate metric used elsewhere), reducing clarity of this section.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning three distinct benchmark families (synthetic T-Maze, 48 POPGym tasks, and MIKASA-Robo visual manipulation), which is more extensive than many memory-RL papers.
Simple, interpretable update rule (LRU with convex blending) accompanied by clean theoretical results on exponential forgetting, half-life, and boundedness of memory embeddings.

Extensive post-hoc interpretability analysis (memory probing, PCA, cross-attention visualization, update-pattern heatmaps) that provides some mechanistic insight into what the memory is actually storing, which is unusual and appreciated rigor for this sub-area.
Reasonably thorough ablation study isolating the contributions of memory capacity, relative bias, LRU mechanism, and shared vs. per-layer memory.
Reproducibility statement and promise of code release; architectural details and hyperparameters are documented in appendix tables.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is incremental: layer-local external memory with read/write cross-attention and LRU eviction closely resembles a combination of well-established ideas (Transformer-XL segment recurrence, NTM/DNC-style external memory, Memformer global slots, Block-Recurrent Transformers), and the paper does not clearly articulate what is fundamentally new beyond re-combining these components with a particular eviction policy.

Headline claims are partly built on a very simple synthetic task (T-Maze), where the only information that must be retained is a single discrete cue; achieving 100% success at corridor length 10^6 is a weak stress-test of 'real' long-horizon memory capability and the '100,000x attention window' framing in the abstract overstates the difficulty/significance of this result.

There are internal inconsistencies in reporting POPGym results: the abstract/intro claim 'top score on 24 of 48 tasks,' while Table 5's caption states ELMUR achieves best performance on only 12 of 21 tasks — these numbers do not reconcile and raise concerns about careful proofreading/reporting of core results.

The claimed ~70% aggregate improvement on MIKASA-Robo is computed over a sum that includes many tasks where every method (including ELMUR) scores exactly 0.00±0.00 (e.g., BunchOfColors, SeqOfColors, ChainOfColors families), meaning the relative percentage gain is sensitive to a few outlier tasks and to baseline near-zero performance rather than reflecting broad-based superiority; a more honest metric (e.g., gains restricted to solvable tasks, or statistical significance testing) is needed.

The improvement over the most relevant and closest prior baseline with explicit memory (RATE) is often modest (e.g., POPGym aggregate 10.4 vs. 9.5, many individual POPGym tasks statistically tied or RATE winning), undermining the strength of the main claims; most of the large reported gains come from comparisons against baselines with no explicit long-term memory (DT, BC, CQL, DP), which is an easier bar to clear on memory-intensive tasks.

The ablation shows that replacing the MoE-FFN with a standard MLP yields identical performance (1.00±0.00) on the probed task, suggesting the MoE component—a nontrivial added complexity/compute cost—is not well-justified or ablated across the other benchmarks where it might matter more.

No real-robot or online RL evaluation is included (explicitly excluded), and no comparison to more modern long-context/memory baselines mentioned in the related work (e.g., Titans, AMAGO-2, Memorizing Transformers, S4/Mamba variants) is provided in the main results tables, limiting the strength of the comparative claims.

The paper is unusually long with a sprawling appendix (30+ pages of extra visualizations/probing), which, while interesting, dilutes the core contribution and makes it harder to assess whether the central claims are well supported versus being bolstered by volume of auxiliary analysis.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning four distinct benchmark families (T-Maze, POPGym-48, MIKASA-Robo, D4RL, and ViZDoom-Two-Colors), which is unusually broad for a single paper and provides good evidence of generality across puzzle, control, and robotic manipulation domains.

Strong quantitative results on several axes: 100% success on T-Maze corridors up to one million steps with only a 10-step attention window, best success rate on 21/23 non-trivial MIKASA-Robo tasks, and competitive aggregate POPGym performance.

Formal theoretical analysis (exponential forgetting with explicit half-life, and boundedness of memory norms under convex blending) that, while algebraically simple, gives interpretable guarantees connecting the LRU hyperparameter to retention horizon.

Unusually thorough interpretability/probing study in the appendix (linear probing of memory slots, cross-attention visualizations, PCA trajectories, slot update/variance patterns) that provides genuine mechanistic evidence the model is using memory functionally rather than just benefiting from extra parameters.

Reasonable efficiency profile: added memory track does not increase wall-clock cost relative to baselines (ELMUR is reported faster per step than RATE and DT despite more parameters), and the design decouples compute from sequence length.

Comprehensive ablations (memory size M vs required segments N, blending factor λ, initialization scale σ, segment configuration, relative bias, shared vs per-layer memory) that meaningfully probe the design space.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is incremental: layer-local external memory with read/write cross-attention and slot-based replacement is a recombination of well-established ideas (Memformer's global slots, NTM/DNC-style addressable memory, Block-Recurrent Transformers, RMT/RATE's segment recurrence); the main novel ingredients (LRU replacement/blending schedule, relative-bias cross-attention) are relatively small increments over this prior art.

Reported aggregate improvements can be misleading: many MIKASA-Robo tasks (BunchOfColors, SeqOfColors, ChainOfColors) show 0.00 success for every method including ELMUR, so the claimed ~70% aggregate improvement is driven by a subset of tasks and partly reflects baseline failure rather than ELMUR's strength on the full suite.

Results are mixed rather than uniformly dominant: RATE is competitive or better on several POPGym tasks and on ViZDoom-Two-Colors, and ELMUR wins only roughly half of POPGym-48 tasks, which tempers the 'best overall' narrative somewhat.

There is an internal inconsistency in the reported POPGym task counts/subsets (e.g., 'top score on 24 of 48 POPGym tasks' in the main text vs. 'best performance on 12 of 21 tasks' in the appendix table caption), which raises concerns about clarity/consistency of reporting.

The MoE-FFN component, bundled as a core design choice and theoretically featured in the method description, is shown by the ablation to be unnecessary (MoE→MLP preserves accuracy while being more efficient), suggesting it is extraneous complexity rather than a validated contribution.

The 'memory horizon extension' claim is partly an expected consequence of standard segment-level recurrence with a correctly sized number of slots (M must scale with number of segments N, as shown in ablations); framing this as a 100,000x extension somewhat overstates a property that is largely by construction rather than an emergent capability.

No real-robot evaluation and no comparison against more modern/competitive external-memory VLA baselines discussed extensively in the related work (e.g., MemoryVLA, SAM2Act, RATE-based VLA variants), limiting the demonstrated significance for practical robot deployment.

Reproducibility artifacts are incomplete in the submission (project page/code link is blank, '.' placeholder), and statistical evaluation relies on only 3-4 seeds without significance testing despite substantial variance in several result tables.
